title: Shared working habits, a written charter and what conflict teaches
moduleTitle: Shared: Growing and managing a team
audience: Team leaders who form a new crew, or who want an existing crew to agree on how it works together.
learningOutcomes: Write team norms that are specific enough to spot a deviation.
Draft a short team charter that includes how conflict will be handled.
Describe how a crew should learn from a conflict after it has been resolved.

instruction.heading: Why norms are written down
instruction.body: Every crew develops habits. Some are helpful, such as a radio check at the start of each job. Others are harmful, such as leaving a problem for the next shift. Written norms make the expected habits visible. They also become a yardstick. When someone does something that does not match a norm, it is easier to raise it calmly because the expectation was agreed in advance.

instruction.heading: A charter that plans for trouble
instruction.body: A charter records why the crew exists, its norms, its roles, how decisions get made and how conflict is handled. Conflict will happen even in a good crew, so agree early how it will be raised and by when it will be addressed. Teams that discuss their working habits openly at the start tend to deal with problems sooner. Agreeing these habits is not always comfortable, but the discomfort is smaller than the cost of unspoken friction.

instruction.heading: Learning from conflict and the human side
instruction.body: Even small conflicts create discomfort. After a disagreement is settled, ask the crew what the norms need to say to prevent it next time. Protect a few minutes for the individual alongside the job itself: a brief check-in at the start of a shift often shows that a worker is struggling with something outside work. Address that first, then plan the job. A crew that feels heard is more willing to follow the norms when a hard day comes.

procedure: Write three to five norms, each one stated as an observable behaviour.
Draft the charter headings: purpose, norms, roles, decisions, conflict handling and review date.
Agree the conflict handling steps with the crew: who speaks first, how quickly, and where the discussion happens.
Run a start-of-shift check-in for two weeks and note any concern raised.
After any conflict is settled, check whether a norm needs to be clearer.
Review the charter at the agreed date and update it with the crew.

workedExamples.situation: A new residential crew of five agrees on norms but two members argue about who should lock the client's door after each job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What norm and conflict step would prevent the argument next time?
workedExamples.reasoning: The crew writes a specific norm: the last person out checks and confirms the door on the job sheet. The conflict step says the lead raises any disagreement at the next briefing rather than on the client's site. The check-in each morning gives the crew a chance to raise any issue early.

equipmentAndPpe: Charter template or whiteboard. Standard PPE on site.

commonErrors.error: Writing norms that are vague, such as 'be a good team player', so no one can tell when they are broken.
commonErrors.prevention: State each norm as a behaviour that can be seen.

commonErrors.error: Writing a charter once and never using it.
commonErrors.prevention: Review the charter on a date and use it at briefings.

commonErrors.error: Dealing with conflict on the client's site.
commonErrors.prevention: Agree that disagreements are raised at a briefing or a private moment, not in front of the client.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A norm must never require a worker to skip a safety step or a site rule.

qualityStandard: The charter has the six headings and each norm is an observable behaviour.
The crew has agreed the conflict handling steps and the review date.
documentationEvidence: Signed or initialled team charter with the review date.
Check-in log showing concerns raised and actions taken.
summary: Norms make expected habits visible and give a yardstick for deviations.
A charter agrees how conflict will be raised before conflict happens.
After a conflict, check whether a norm needs clearer wording.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which norm is written well enough to spot a deviation?
options: Be a good team player and always be happy with the work and the pay
Work hard and keep the team talking through each room and keep it up all the time
The last person out checks and confirms the client's door on the job sheet
Get along with everyone and make friends with the client and the family

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a crew agree conflict handling in advance?
options: So the lead does not need to be involved in any dispute on any job at all
So conflicts can be kept off the record and nobody needs to write it down
So the client sees every disagreement as it happens and can comment on it
So the crew knows how and when a disagreement will be addressed before it happens

knowledgeChecks.question: A new crew member appears to be struggling with a personal problem at the start of a shift. What fits the lesson best?
options: Address the person first with a brief check-in, then plan the work
Start the job and leave the matter for the end of the week
Send the person home immediately without discussion today
Note it and say nothing to anyone on the crew at all today
